name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,822

entries.clue: Imagine Labour's behind, with Conservative party leading (8)

indicatorNotes.behind: A person's behind is their rear end, so Labour gives up the letter at its rear.
indicatorNotes.leading: Whatever is leading goes at the head of the column, so the two chunks named alongside it are entered first.

blocks.note: Con is how the Conservative party is printed on an election-night tally
a party to a quarrel is one side of it
the letter Labour ends on

annotation.surface: Labour trailing in the polls while the Conservatives move into the lead.
annotation.walkthrough: The two parties do quite different jobs: one hands over its short form, the other only the letter it finishes on. 'Party' is wanted in the older sense, a side in a dispute.
annotation.definitionFit: To consider a course of action is to imagine it, turning the possibility over in the mind before deciding.

entries.clue: In Rome, one editor surplus to requirements (6)

blocks.note: unus is the Latin for one, and Rome is the setter asking for Latin
ed is the short form on a letters page

annotation.surface: A Roman editor who turns out not to be needed after all.
annotation.walkthrough: Naming a country or city is a standing way of asking for that language rather than English, and it is worth watching for wherever a clue mentions one. The definition is the phrase used when a job is cut.
annotation.definitionFit: Stock that is surplus to requirements is never drawn on and sits in the warehouse unused, the word and the phrase both saying nothing was called for.

entries.clue: Dog raised knowing right from wrong in royal palace (8)

indicatorNotes.raised: In a down entry, letters that are raised are lifted up the grid, so they read from the bottom upwards.

blocks.note: a Lab is the retriever, here climbing the grid
a moral sense is what tells right from wrong

annotation.surface: A dog brought up to know right from wrong at a royal residence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Raised' reads as brought up, which is how you would describe a well-trained dog, and it is the order to turn letters upward. Lab is the crossword's usual dog, short for Labrador.
annotation.definitionFit: Balmoral is the monarch's castle in Aberdeenshire, the royal family's Highland home every summer since Victoria bought the estate in 1852.

entries.clue: Car in cemetery tries heading for exit (6)

indicatorNotes.heading for: The heading of a word is the letter it starts with, so only that opening letter of what follows is taken.

blocks.note: a judge tries a case by hearing it
the letter exit begins with

annotation.surface: A car stuck in a cemetery, looking for the way out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tries' sounds like an attempt and is the courtroom verb instead. The definition is the whole opening phrase rather than its first word, which is why the clue seems to have a spare noun in it.
annotation.definitionFit: A hearse is the long black car that carries the coffin to the cemetery, so the clue's car is one in its working place.

entries.clue: Reason golf has 18 holes? (6)

blocks.note: golf is G in the radio alphabet
a full circuit of a course, eighteen holes, is a round

annotation.surface: Wondering why a game of golf runs to eighteen holes.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark owns up to the surface asking something golfers genuinely ask. 'Golf' is the radio-alphabet letter, even though the game supplies the rest of the wordplay as well.
annotation.definitionFit: A ground for suspicion is a reason for it, the singular noun surviving mainly in that legal-sounding phrase.

entries.clue: Englishman in Mexico, perhaps good drummer (6)

blocks.note: g is the mark for good on a school report
Ringo Starr drummed for the Beatles

annotation.surface: An Englishman living in Mexico who is rated a good drummer.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition runs to four words and 'perhaps' does the conceding: the answer covers any English-speaking outsider, not Englishmen alone. Ringo is the crossword's standing drummer.
annotation.definitionFit: Gringo is Latin American Spanish for a foreigner, usually an English-speaking one, so an Englishman in Mexico is one instance of the breed.

entries.clue: Pet is concerned to get a bit of sausage (6)

indicatorNotes.a bit of: A bit of a thing is a small part of it, and the smallest part of a written word is the letter it opens with.

blocks.note: somebody who is concerned about a thing cares about it
the letter sausage starts with

annotation.surface: The family pet, anxious for its scrap of sausage.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pet' opens the clue looking like the animal in the kitchen and is the verb, to stroke. That is why the definition is one word and the sausage comes to nothing but its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To pet an animal is to caress it, both verbs meaning to stroke with affection.

entries.clue: Event where people talk, therefore spies left (6)

blocks.note: so is the everyday word for therefore
the CIA is the American intelligence agency
l is left on a map or a stage direction

annotation.surface: Spies walking out of a gathering because too much gets said at one.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma invites you to read the tail as the consequence of all that talking, and all three of those words are separate letter-chunks. CIA is the crossword's default set of spies.
annotation.definitionFit: A social is an informal gathering — the church-hall or club sort of evening — laid on for company and conversation rather than any other purpose.

entries.clue: Secretive Scottish family all but doomed (11)

indicatorNotes.all but: All but the whole of a thing is nearly all of it, so the word named gives up its last letter.

blocks.note: a clan is the Scottish family group, Campbell or MacDonald
somebody doomed is destined for a particular end, and the final D falls away

annotation.surface: A Scottish family on the brink of dying out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'All but doomed' reads as one phrase meaning nearly finished and splits into an instruction and the word it acts on. Doomed and destined are the same idea: a fate already fixed.
annotation.definitionFit: A clandestine meeting is arranged in secret and kept that way, which is the hidden quality 'secretive' names.

entries.clue: Feel the loss of American wife (6)

blocks.note: to miss somebody is to feel their absence
US is the standard short form of the United States

annotation.surface: A man pining for his American wife.
annotation.walkthrough: The sentence runs straight through as one thought about grief, with the definition the single word at the end. The answer is spoken British English — 'I'll ask the missus' — rather than anything you would write down.
annotation.definitionFit: The missus is British informal speech for a man's wife, the word a husband uses for her in the pub.

entries.clue: Creamed rice and milk, type Lear liked? (8)

indicatorNotes.Creamed: Cream something and it is beaten smooth with nothing left where it began, so the letters named take a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: A creamy rice pudding of the sort a Victorian poet was fond of.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Type' points at a form of verse rather than a sort of pudding, and Lear is the nonsense poet, not a diner. The fodder steps over the word 'and', which hides where the letters begin and end.
annotation.definitionFit: Edward Lear filled his Book of Nonsense with five-line verses, so the limerick is the type that Victorian poet liked.

entries.clue: Silver Edward kept in storage for a time (4)

annotation.definition: kept in storage for a time

blocks.note: Ag is silver's symbol on the periodic table
Ed is the short form of the name

annotation.surface: Edward's silver, put away in store for years.
annotation.walkthrough: Chemical symbols are the setter's shortest route to a metal, and silver's comes from argentum rather than the English word. The definition is what a distiller does to whisky, holding it in cask until it is ready.
annotation.definitionFit: Whisky or cheese held in store until it matures is described as aged, the word covering exactly that spell put by.

entries.clue: Hot sandwich made by inventive baker - bravo (5,5)

indicatorNotes.inventive: An inventive cook makes something new out of whatever is to hand, so the letters named are put together in another order.

blocks.note: a thing already made is done
the six letters of BAKER plus the B that bravo stands for in the radio alphabet, rearranged

annotation.surface: A hot snack dreamed up by a creative baker, and a cheer for him.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash lets 'bravo' pass for applause while it hands over a radio-alphabet letter. The rearranged letters straddle the gap between the answer's two words, so the break falls where no clue word suggests it.
annotation.definitionFit: A doner kebab is meat carved off the spit into a pitta and sold hot from a takeaway, which is a sandwich in all but name.

entries.clue: Concrete wind break? (6,5)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Concrete' is the material rather than the object, an adjective standing for the noun it makes up — the licence setters take with building stuff.

blocks.note: a breeze is a light wind
a break put up on a beach is a barrier, and to block is to stop a thing the same way

annotation.surface: A concrete screen put up to keep the wind off.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark owns up to the joke: both halves read as stopping the wind, while the answer is an item off a builder's merchant's pallet. Breeze was the ash and cinder those blocks were first made with.
annotation.definitionFit: A breeze block is the grey building block cast from lightweight concrete, so 'concrete' names what one is made of.

entries.clue: Train tours are subject to alteration (8)

indicatorNotes.subject to alteration: Anything subject to alteration may be changed about, so the letters named are free to take a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: Rail holidays the operator may change without notice.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the first word and the rest is booking-terms boilerplate, which is why no part of the sentence sounds like an instruction. The service meant runs under the Channel from St Pancras to Paris.
annotation.definitionFit: Eurostar is the passenger train through the Channel Tunnel, so 'train' is the plain class it belongs to.

entries.clue: Improvised recital includes new instrument (8)

indicatorNotes.Improvised: An improvised piece is played in no set order, so the letters named come out rearranged.
indicatorNotes.includes: What a thing includes is part of it, so the letter named joins the pile being rearranged rather than sitting outside it.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
n is the standard short form of new

annotation.surface: A recital played off the cuff, with a new instrument in the programme.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Improvised' passes as praise for the playing and is the shuffle. 'Includes' is the join, telling you the extra letter goes into the pile rather than round the outside of it.
annotation.definitionFit: The clarinet is the single-reed woodwind of the orchestra and the dance band, so 'instrument' is its plain class word.

entries.clue: Drink can go cold when served up (6)

indicatorNotes.served up: Food served up is sent upwards to the table, and up in a down entry means the letters are read from the bottom of the pile to the top.

blocks.note: the word itself, taken whole
the word itself, taken whole
c is cold on a tap or a washing-machine dial

annotation.surface: A drink that will go cold if it stands about after being served.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word of the wordplay is pulling its weight in a sentence about a drink left standing, and only 'served up' is an instruction. The spirit is named after the town in western France where it is distilled.
annotation.definitionFit: Cognac is the brandy distilled around that town in the Charente, so 'drink' is the plainest possible label for it.

entries.clue: Graduate bank with nothing to spare (6)

blocks.note: a BA is the arts degree a graduate comes out with
to bank on somebody is to rely on them

annotation.surface: A graduate banking what little money he has left.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bank' is the verb, to depend, not the building the graduate walks into. The definition is the whole tail of the clue, an adverbial phrase where a single word would do.
annotation.definitionFit: A team that wins with nothing to spare barely wins, both saying the margin was the smallest there is.

entries.clue: E.g. Bob Dylan back in Bognor Regis, town going wild (10)

indicatorNotes.back in: What stands at the back in a word is its closing letter, so Bognor gives up that one letter.
indicatorNotes.going wild: A crowd going wild breaks out of all order, so the letters named are rearranged.

blocks.note: the letter Bognor ends on
anagram fodder, nine letters, with the letter above making ten

annotation.surface: Bob Dylan playing Bognor Regis again, with the town going crazy for him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back in Bognor' reads as a return visit and yields one letter, which is why the anagram comes up short if you start from the resort's name alone. Bognor Regis is a seaside town on the Sussex coast.
annotation.definitionFit: Bob Dylan writes the words and music of his own songs, so he is one example of the class the answer names, which is what the 'e.g.' signals.

entries.clue: Horse found in the middle of hunting-grounds? (3-3)

indicatorNotes.in the middle of: The middle of a word is its dead centre, so the letters taken are the ones with equal numbers either side.

blocks.note: the fourteen letters have G and G at their exact centre, one on each side of the hyphen, and those two letters are written out by name

annotation.surface: A horse wandering loose in the middle of the hunting grounds.
annotation.walkthrough: Count the letters of the hyphenated word and the dead centre falls on the hyphen itself, with the same letter on either side of it. The question mark covers the last step, spelling those letters out as they are said.
annotation.definitionFit: A gee-gee is a horse in British nursery talk and racecourse slang — a flutter on the gee-gees — from the 'gee up' called to start one moving.

entries.clue: Slice of meat wrapped by butcher as he recommended (6)

indicatorNotes.wrapped by: What is wrapped by something is tucked away inside it, so the answer lies buried in the words that follow.

blocks.note: running on from the end of butcheR through AS HE to the start of Recommended

annotation.surface: A cut of meat the butcher wrapped up and spoke well of.
annotation.walkthrough: The hidden run crosses three word-breaks, and 'as he recommended' is exactly the sort of filler a solver's eye skates over — which is where the letters are sitting.
annotation.definitionFit: A rasher is the single slice of bacon that goes into the pan, so 'slice of meat' is its everyday job.

entries.clue: Unfortunately a girl loses one shilling (4)

indicatorNotes.loses: What a word loses it no longer has, so the letter named is taken out of it.

blocks.note: lass is the northern word for a girl, and the clue's own 'a' stands in front of it
s was the short form printed against a price in shillings, and one of the two Ss goes

annotation.surface: A girl unlucky enough to drop a shilling.
annotation.walkthrough: Shillings were written s — twelve pence to one, twenty to the pound — until decimal currency came in in 1971. 'One' is doing real work here: there are two of that letter and only one of them leaves.
annotation.definitionFit: Alas is how you say a thing is unfortunate, an old-fashioned sigh that still opens a sentence where 'unfortunately' would.

entries.clue: Fairy-tale writer with Irish name (8)

blocks.note: and joins two things the way with does
Erse is the old English name for the Irish Gaelic tongue
n is the standard short form of name

annotation.surface: A writer of fairy tales who happens to have an Irish name.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like the hinge of the sentence and is three letters of the answer. Erse is a setter's favourite for Irish, and comes up far more often in crosswords than in conversation.
annotation.definitionFit: Hans Christian Andersen wrote The Ugly Duckling, The Snow Queen and The Little Mermaid, which makes him the fairy-tale writer of the clue.

entries.clue: Dirty son covered with grease (6)

blocks.note: s is the short form of son on a family tree
something covered with grease is oiled

annotation.surface: A son who has come in from the garage covered in grease.
annotation.walkthrough: The adjective at the front is the definition and the rest describes the same boy in the same state, so no part of the sentence stands out as wordplay. The answer is the word on a laundry basket rather than one you would say aloud.
annotation.definitionFit: Soiled linen is dirty linen, the word being the polite label the hotel puts on the basket.

entries.clue: "Arrest that woman," said man attacked in Senate (6)

indicatorNotes.said: Said points at how words sound rather than how they are spelt, so the order in quotes is to be heard and not read.

blocks.note: the order to arrest a woman is 'seize her', two words that run together into the name

annotation.surface: An officer barking out an order to arrest a woman.
annotation.walkthrough: The quoted order is spoken, which is what makes the sound fair, and 'said' is the only word telling you so. The man of the definition was stabbed by senators in Rome on the Ides of March, 44 BC.
annotation.definitionFit: Julius Caesar was set upon by a group of senators and stabbed to death at a meeting of the Senate, the most famous attack in Roman history.

entries.clue: Cure connected with year by the sea (6)

blocks.note: re heads a memo about something, meaning connected with it
the Med is what British holidaymakers call the Mediterranean
y is the short form of year in a date

annotation.surface: A cure that amounts to a year spent beside the sea.
annotation.walkthrough: A year by the sea does sound curative, which is why the sentence hangs together so quietly. The two letters at the front come from the memo heading, not from anything the surface is describing.
annotation.definitionFit: A remedy is the thing that puts an ailment right, standing where 'cure' would in a phrase like a cure for hiccups.
